title: Hannibal's Trap at Cannae
text:
On 2 August 216 BC, near the village of Cannae in southern Italy, the largest army Rome had ever fielded faced Hannibal. The Romans, under the consuls Varro and Aemilius Paullus, had roughly eighty thousand men. Hannibal had about fifty thousand, but more and better cavalry.

Polybius describes Hannibal's deployment. He placed his Gallic and Spanish infantry in the center in a line that bulged forward toward the Romans. On each side of them, set back, stood his veteran African infantry. His cavalry held the wings. The Romans, trusting in weight, packed their legions deep and narrow and pushed straight at the center.

The bulge gave ground slowly as planned, bending back into a hollow. The Roman mass followed it in, pressing tighter. Then the African infantry on either side turned inward and attacked the Roman flanks. Meanwhile Hannibal's cavalry, under Hasdrubal, had routed the Roman horse and swung around to strike the Roman rear. The Romans were surrounded and so crowded that many could not use their weapons.

Polybius says about seventy thousand Romans died, including Paullus, while Hannibal lost under six thousand. Cannae became the textbook example of encirclement, studied by generals for two thousand years.
lesson: Let an opponent's strength carry him where you want him. A part that yields on purpose can be the hinge of the whole plan.
people: Hannibal Barca, Hasdrubal, Gaius Terentius Varro, Lucius Aemilius Paullus
source: Polybius, Histories 3.107 to 3.117; Livy, History of Rome, book 22
caveat: Ancient casualty figures for Cannae are likely inflated; modern estimates vary.
